His saying, the Exalted: ﴿By the heaven and the Tariq (the night-comer)﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-Tariq is the star. It is so named because it "knocks" (yatruq), that is, it rises at night, and whoever comes to you at night has "knocked" on you (taraqaka). From this is the saying of Hind bint Utbah:

"We are the daughters of Tariq, walking upon the cushions."

She means: our father is a star in his nobility and eminence.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And what will make you know what the Tariq is?﴾ The commentators said: this is because the name applies to everything that comes at night, so the Prophet ﷺ did not know what was meant by it until He explained it with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The piercing star﴾, meaning the luminous one, as we explained in [al-Saffat: 10].

Regarding the referent of this star there are three opinions.

The first: that it is Saturn (Zuhal). This was said by ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him. Abu al-Jawza' narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: It is Zuhal, and its dwelling is in the seventh heaven, which no other star inhabits. When the stars take their places in the sky, it descends and is with them, then it returns to its place in the seventh heaven. So it is a Tariq when it descends, and a Tariq when it ascends.

The second: that it is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: that it is a generic noun (ism jins), mentioned by ʿAli ibn Ahmad al-Naysaburi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There is no soul but that over it is a guardian﴾. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Abu al-Mutawakkil read "inna" with tashdid and "kull" in the accusative. Abu Jaʿfar, Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim al-Jahdari, Hamzah, and Abu Hatim from Yaʿqub read "lamma" with tashdid. The rest read it with takhfif. Al-Zajjaj said: this verse is the response to the oath. Whoever reads it with takhfif, the meaning is: "over it is a guardian," and "ma" is redundant (laghw). Whoever reads it with tashdid, the meaning is "except" (illa). He said: "lamma" is used in the sense of "illa" in two places. One of them is this, and the other is in the matter of oaths. You say: "I asked you, lamma you did it," meaning "illa you did it." The commentators said: the meaning is: there is no soul except that over it is a guardian. On this there are two views.

The first: that they are the recording angels (al-hafazah) from among the angels, said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Qatadah said: they guard the person's deeds, whether good or evil.

The second: a guardian who protects the person until the moment he delivers him to the decrees (al-maqadir), said by al-Farra'.

Then He drew attention to the resurrection with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾, that is, from what thing Allah created him? The meaning: let him look with the look of reflection and inference, so that he may know that the One who originated him from a drop is able to restore him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿From a gushing fluid﴾. Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "maduq" (poured out), like the Arabic expressions "a hidden secret" (sirr katim), "a tiring worry" (hamm nasib), "a sleeping night" (layl na'im), and "a pleasing life" (ʿisha radiyah). The people of the Hijaz make the passive form an active one. Al-Zajjaj said: the view of Sibawayh and his companions is that its meaning is a nisba (attribution) to emission (al-indifaq), and the meaning is: from a fluid having emission.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It emerges from between the loins and the ribs﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Sirin, Ibn al-Sumayfa, and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "al-sulub" with damm on both the sad and the lam. The meaning is: it emerges from the loins of the man and the ribs (taraʾib) of the woman. Al-Farra' said: he means it emerges from the loins and the ribs. It is said: "good much emerges from between these two things," meaning "from them."

Regarding "taraʾib" there are three opinions.

The first: that it is the place of the necklace, said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Zajjaj said: all the lexicographers said: "taraʾib" is the place of the necklace on the chest, and they cited the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"Slender, fair, not overlapping; her taraʾib polished like the sajanjal."

I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur the lexicographer, who said: al-sajanjal is a mirror in Rumi (Greek/Byzantine). It is also said: it is an ingot of silver; it is also said: al-sajanjal is saffron; and it is also said: gold water. The line is also narrated with "bil-sajanjal."

The second: that the taraʾib are the two hands, the two legs, and the two eyes. This was narrated by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Dahhak said the same.

The third: that they are four ribs on the right side of the chest and four ribs on the left side of the chest, related by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed He is over its return﴾. The pronoun refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Over its return (raj'ihi)﴾. The raj' is returning a thing to its original state. Regarding this pronoun there are two views.

The first: that it refers to the human being. Then there are two views on this. One: that He is able to restore the human being alive after his death, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. Al-Zajjaj said: this view is supported by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On the day when secrets are examined﴾. The second: that He is able to return him from the state of old age to youth, from youth to childhood, and from childhood to the drop, said by al-Dahhak.

The second view: that the pronoun refers to the water. Then there are three views on the meaning. One: the return of the water into the urethra, said by Mujahid. The second: its return into the loins, said by ʿIkrimah and al-Dahhak. The third: the holding back of the water so that it does not emerge, said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On the day when secrets are examined﴾. The secrets that lie between the servant and his Lord, until the good in them is distinguished from the evil, and the one who performed them from the one who neglected them. For a person is concealed in this world; he does not know whether he prayed or not, or whether he performed ablution or not. But when the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will reveal every secret, and it will be an adornment to the face or a blemish. Ibn Qutaybah said: the secrets of hearts are tested.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then he will have no power﴾, that is, this human being who denies the resurrection will have no power by which he may protect himself from the punishment of Allah, ﴿nor any helper﴾ to aid him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 86, verse 11–17:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿By the sky, which returns [rain]﴾. That is, possessor of rain (dhat al-matar). Rain is called raj'an (return) because it comes, returns, and recurs. ﴿And [by] the earth, which splits [with growth]﴾. That is, possessor of splitting (dhat al-shaqq). It has been said that it is so called because it splits and cracks open with vegetation. This is the saying of the exegetes (mufassirun) and the lexicographers (ahl al-lughah) regarding the two words.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾. He means by it the Qur'an, and this is the answer to the oath. The fasl (decisive) is that which distinguishes between truth and falsehood through clarification of each of them. ﴿And it is not a jest﴾. That is, it is not play. The meaning is that it is serious, and it was not sent down in play. Some say the pronoun in "innahu" refers to the threat mentioned earlier.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they﴾ — meaning the polytheists of Makkah — ﴿are plotting a plot﴾ [that is, they are scheming]. This scheming is the plotting against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when they gathered in Dar al-Nadwah. ﴿And I am plotting a plot﴾. That is, I will repay them [for their plot] by leading them step by step from where they do not know, so I will take vengeance upon them in this world by the sword and in the Hereafter by the Fire. ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers﴾. This is a threat from Allah against them. Mahhil and amhil are two dialects combined here. The meaning of the verse: give them a little respite until I destroy them. When "amhil-hum" does not precede it, it carries the meaning of "mahlan." It is not used except diminutive (musaghghara) and as a command, but it came in poetry without diminutive, in a sense other than command.

The poet said:

؎ As if she were like one who walks upon ruwd

That is, upon slowness (ala mahl).

The poet said:

؎ As if she were like one who walks upon ruwd

That is, upon slowness (ala mahl).

It has been said that it is so called because it splits and cracks open with vegetation. This is the saying of the exegetes (mufassirun) and the lexicographers (ahl al-lughah) regarding the two words.
